origin_region: Kyoto · Uji, Wazuka and the southern Yamashiro hills
processing: Large, mature leaves and twigs are cut from the bushes (often when the plants are pruned after the first flush), steamed, dried flat without rolling, then roasted hard over high heat, which gives the tea its smoky, scorched aroma.
harvest_season: Cut after the first flush in late spring or early summer, and again when the bushes are pruned in autumn; made from leaf that would otherwise be waste.
appearance_dry: Big, flat, whole dried leaves and twig pieces in brown and dark olive, crisp and papery, taking up a lot of space.
appearance_wet: Large, leathery brown-green leaves that look like fallen leaves after rain.
taste_profile: Campfire smoke and toasted straw with a light, dry, almost savoury body and no astringency; the aroma is the whole experience.

brewing.notes: Boil it: a large handful in a kettle or big pot with boiling water for a couple of minutes, or simmer briefly, then drink hot or chilled. A small kyusu is pointless because the leaves are so bulky; one re-steep is possible.

vintage_note: A cheap everyday tea sold in big bags all year round by Kyoto shops and supermarkets, with no vintage or grade beyond the house's roast; the smoky aroma is strongest in the first months after roasting and softens over a year. It is not aged on purpose but keeps far longer than green sencha, so a bag in the cupboard for a year is still fine.
description:
Kyōbancha is Kyoto's everyday bancha and it smells like a bonfire. It is made from big, mature leaves and twigs, dried flat without rolling and then roasted hard, and the result is a light, dry, smoky tea that Kyoto households drink by the kettleful, serve to children and keep chilled in summer. People either love it on the first sip or need a week to come round.

The leaf is cut from the bushes after the first flush, when the plants are pruned, so it is leaf that would otherwise go to waste. It is steamed, spread out to dry whole, like fallen leaves, and then roasted in a pan or drum until it browns and some of it scorches; the smoke is a product of the roast, not of any wood smoke, so the aroma is dry and toasty rather than tarry. Mature leaf plus a hard roast means very little caffeine and no astringency to speak of.

Forget the kyusu. The leaves are so bulky that a small pot holds only a pinch; instead put a big handful (about 10 g) in a kettle or large teapot with half a litre of boiling water, give it a couple of minutes or a brief simmer, and drink it hot or pour it into a jug for the fridge. It makes a surprisingly good cold tea, and it can be re-steeped once. Brewed cool and short like sencha it tastes of nothing, which is the usual mistake made by people who treat every Japanese tea the same way.

Kyoto shops and supermarkets sell it in large, light bags for very little money; the label may say kyōbancha or iribancha and that is about all the grading there is. Look for whole, intact leaves and not much dust, and buy from a shop that roasts regularly, because the smoky aroma is strongest in the months after roasting. It keeps far longer than green sencha, so a year in the cupboard does no harm.

Drink it with oily or heavy food, or as a near-caffeine-free nightcap; and if you want a comparison, Mimasaka bancha from Okayama and ordinary hōjicha are its two nearest cousins.
